charts.title: Net Income vs Free Cash Flow vs Owner FCF
charts.annotation: Owner FCF, where shown, is the DCF's series after SBC, interest income and lease principal. "FCF (JD reported)" is JD's own cash-flow-statement FCF and can diverge sharply from OCF-less-CapEx -- e.g. FY2018 was negative on JD's definition but positive on the simple OCF-CapEx calculation.

balanceSheet.title: Balance sheet
balanceSheet.content:
Shareholders' equity is assets less liabilities; plotted against total liabilities to show leverage.

For JD.com, Inc.: equity that grows only through revaluations or share issues is not the same as retained earnings.

What to watch:

  • Liabilities growing faster than equity
  • Goodwill share of equity after acquisitions

cashDebt.title: Cash and debt
cashDebt.content:
Cash & equivalents against total borrowings (leases excluded unless noted).

For JD.com, Inc.: the DCF's net-debt bridge uses these balances at the latest balance-sheet date.

What to watch:

  • Net debt trend versus EBITDA
  • Refinancing dates and covenants in the filings

ebitda.title: EBITDA
ebitda.content:
EBITDA is earnings before interest, tax, depreciation and amortisation -- an operating-cash proxy that ignores capital intensity.

For JD.com, Inc.: read it beside CapEx: a business that must reinvest most of its EBITDA is not as cash-generative as the margin suggests.

What to watch:

  • EBITDA margin trend
  • Gap between EBITDA and operating cash flow (working capital)

epsDps.title: EPS and dividends
epsDps.content:
EPS is net income per share; DPS is the cash dividend paid per share. Both are in major currency units.

For JD.com, Inc.: this EPS is per Class A ordinary share. JD's ADS (the Nasdaq-quoted unit, ticker JD) equals 2 ordinary shares, so diluted EPS per ADS is simply double this figure -- e.g. FY2025's CNY6.45 here is CNY12.90 per ADS. The DCF's per-share outputs are already stated on the ADS basis.

What to watch:

  • EPS growth versus net income growth (dilution)
  • Dividends funded from earnings, not debt

fcf.title: Free cash flow
fcf.content:
FCF (OCF less CapEx) is operating cash flow minus capital expenditure, computed the same way across every ticker on this site. FCF (JD reported) is JD's own cash-flow-statement free cash flow, which can use a different CapEx scope (e.g. only property/equipment, excluding other investing items this chart's simple formula nets off). Owner FCF (from the DCF) further deducts stock-based compensation, interest income and lease principal -- the cash an owner could actually take out.

For JD.com, Inc.: the two FCF lines diverge sharply in some years -- FY2018 is negative on JD's own definition but positive on the OCF-less-CapEx calculation -- so check which one a guidance statement refers to before comparing it to this chart.

What to watch:

  • FCF persistently below net income
  • Working-capital swings inflating one year's FCF
  • Years where the two FCF definitions disagree in sign, not just magnitude

margins.title: Margins
margins.content:
Gross margin is revenue less cost of revenue; operating margin deducts operating expenses; net margin is after interest and tax.

For JD.com, Inc.: the spread between gross and operating margin is the cost of running the business; a widening spread with flat gross margin means opex is growing faster than sales.

What to watch:

  • Direction of operating margin over several years, not one
  • One-offs (impairments, disposals) that distort net margin

ocfCapex.title: Operating cash flow and CapEx
ocfCapex.content:
Operating cash flow is cash generated by operations; CapEx is cash invested in fixed and intangible assets.

For JD.com, Inc.: CapEx here is shown as stored (sign convention varies by ticker); the DCF splits it into stay-in-business and growth where disclosed.

What to watch:

  • CapEx rising faster than revenue
  • OCF that diverges from EBITDA

profit.title: Profit lines
profit.content:
Gross profit is revenue less cost of revenue; operating income deducts operating expenses; net income is after interest, tax and one-offs.

For JD.com, Inc.: the three lines together show where margin is made and lost between the top line and the bottom.

What to watch:

  • Operating income growing slower than gross profit (opex creep)
  • Net income far from operating income (interest, tax, one-offs)

segmentRevenue.title: Segment revenue
segmentRevenue.content:
JD reports two main segments: JD Retail, the self-operated e-commerce business (1P merchandise sales plus marketplace/advertising), and JD Logistics, the supply-chain and delivery network JD increasingly sells to external customers rather than using purely in-house.

For JD.com, Inc.: JD Retail still dwarfs Logistics in revenue, but Logistics has grown faster off external contracts -- a different, more capital-intensive, lower-margin business than the retail arm. A small third segment, New Businesses (Jingxi, overseas units, Dada), is omitted here as immaterial.

What to watch:

  • JD Logistics revenue growth versus JD Retail -- is logistics becoming a real second business or just an internal cost centre?
  • External-customer share of JD Logistics revenue (not broken out in the CSV)

segmentOperatingIncome.title: Segment operating income
segmentOperatingIncome.content:
Operating income for the same two segments. JD Logistics is a lower-margin, asset-heavy network (warehouses, delivery fleet) that spent years scaling before turning profitable.

For JD.com, Inc.: JD Logistics ran at an operating loss through FY2021 and has been profitable every full year since FY2022 -- the key inflection for whether the external-logistics business adds or subtracts from group earnings.

What to watch:

  • JD Logistics operating margin versus JD Retail's (structurally much thinner)
  • Whether JD Logistics profitability holds through a slower parcel-volume year

revenue.title: Revenue
revenue.content:
Revenue is the top line: what customers paid for goods and services in the period, before any costs.

For JD.com, Inc.: the growth rate matters more than the level; compare it with the DCF's base-case growth path below.

What to watch:

  • Acceleration or deceleration in YoY growth
  • Whether growth is organic or acquired
  • Interim rows show seasonality

sbc.title: Stock-based compensation and share count
sbc.content:
Stock-based comp is the expense of equity awards; shares outstanding shows the dilution it causes net of buybacks.

For JD.com, Inc.: the DCF charges SBC as a cash cost and holds the share count flat, so this chart is the check on that assumption.

What to watch:

  • Share count rising while buybacks are advertised
  • SBC as a percentage of revenue
